about: The last of the three prayers, and the one that names the danger. St Paul writes that whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself — iudicium sibi manducat et bibit — and the 1962 missal prints those words as the Epistle for Corpus Christi and for Holy Thursday; the prayer asks that the receiving not turn out that way. It is built on one subject and two verbs pulling against each other, one negative and one positive: let it not come out to judgment, let it profit me instead. Præsúmo says plainly what the priest is doing: taking beforehand what he is not worthy to take.

s01.translation: Let not the partaking of Thy Body, O Lord Iesus Christ, which I, unworthy, presume to receive,

s02.translation: turn out to my judgment and condemnation:

s03.translation: but by Thy loving-kindness let it profit me as a safeguard of mind and body, and as a healing to be received:

s04.translation: Who livest and reignest with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen.

w001.function: Subject of both verbs of the prayer, and held apart from them by everything in between; it does not reach “provéniat” (w014) until the second segment. Whitaker's does not carry the noun percéptio, so the parse rests on Collatinus alone.

w003.function: Agrees with “Córporis” (w002), not with Percéptio: the Body is Thine, the partaking is mine.

w007.function: Neuter, so it points to “Córporis” (w002), not the feminine Percéptio: what he presumes to receive is the Body, not the partaking of it.

w008.function: Latin needs no subject pronoun; it is here to be weighted against the adjective that follows.

w009.function: Nominative, agreeing with “ego” (w008): I, being unworthy — a description of the man doing the taking, set beside the act.

w011.function: Præ and sumo: to take beforehand, to reach for what one is not worthy of. The word admits the audacity rather than excusing it.

w013.function: Dative with “provéniat” (w014): turn out for whom — for me.

w014.function: Pro and vénio, to come forth: the verb of a result, not of a judgment passed. The Communion may come out either way, and the prayer asks which.

w016.function: The word St Paul uses of eating and drinking unworthily.

w018.function: Judgment is the trial, condemnation the sentence; the prayer names both, in that order.

w022.function: Pro tua pietáte: the unworthy man's plea rests not on his own merit but on God's faithfulness — that one word carries the whole petition.

w023.function: The positive counterpart of “provéniat” (w014), sharing the same subject. Prosum is a compound of sum and belongs to no conjugation.

w026.function: A late formation from tueor, to watch over: a thing that guards. It governs the two genitives that follow.

w027.function: Mens is the mind rather than the soul; the pair the prayer sets together is the mind and the body.

w029.function: The prayer asks for the body as well as the mind, and puts the mind first.

w033.function: A gerundive, which is the future passive participle: agreeing with “medélam” (w032), a healing that is to be received. The obligation such forms usually carry is here no more than purpose.

w045.function: Nominative standing with the two verbs, as in the other two prayers: who as God livest and reignest.
